t:
The reports of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia shall not be sold for a price exceeding that approved by the court and for not more than $6.50 per volume.
This title may be cited as the “Judiciary Appropriation Act, 1968”.

fable.w: The section caps the sale price of court reports and gives a short title for an appropriations act. The only decision-maker mentioned is the court itself, which is inside the federal government; the tempting reading that "approved by the court" signals a participatory process fails because no outside party is consulted, heard, or given a right to sue or object.
fable.s: shall not be sold for a price exceeding that approved by the court

qwen_block.w: This section sets a price cap for the sale of court reports. It does not involve any consultation, coordination, or participation with parties outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private entities) in the decision-making process. The only actor mentioned is the court itself, which is part of the federal government.
qwen_block.s: The reports of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia shall not be sold for a price exceeding that approved by the court and for not more than $6.50 per volume.

opus.w: This section caps the sale price of the D.C. Circuit's reports and gives the Act's short title. The only approval comes from the court itself, which is a federal body, so nothing crosses the federal boundary. No comment period, hearing, advisory body, outside consultation or right to sue is created.
opus.b: **Step 1.** The tempting reading is that "approved by the court" is a review step before a decision. It fails because the D.C. Circuit is a federal court, so it is inside the federal government. The rest of the section is a price cap and a short title. No state, company, expert or member of the public takes part in any federal decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section sets a price cap for court reports and states that the price must be approved by the court. It does not require any consultation, public comment, or coordination with outside parties (such as the general public, states, or experts) before the court makes its decision. The approval process is internal to the federal judiciary.
qwen_chat.s: The reports of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia shall not be sold for a price exceeding that approved by the court and for not more than $6.50 per volume.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that setting a price limit involves public participation because it affects the public's ability to purchase reports. However, the text only sets a price cap and does not require any consultation, hearing, or input from the public or outside entities before the court sets the price. The decision is made internally by the court.
